scenario: A customer-support lead on a Team plan wants every agent's Claude chats to follow the same returns policy and reply style.
question: What is the best setup?
options: Ask each agent to paste the returns policy and reply rules at the start of each chat
A shared Project with the policy as knowledge and the reply rules as instructions
Put the returns policy and reply rules in each agent's account instructions
Email the policy to each agent to upload whenever a returns question comes in
explanation: B is correct: a Project bundles instructions and knowledge, so each agent's chat in it starts from the same policy and rules. A is wrong because repeated pasting drifts, and busy agents skip it. C is wrong because account instructions apply to all of an agent's chats, and each copy goes out of date separately. D is wrong because ad hoc uploads leave each chat with whichever version that agent kept.

scenario: A translation agency on a paid plan keeps its client glossaries and style guides in one Project. The knowledge is nearly at the context limit, so the team plans to delete older reference files to make room.
question: What should the team do?
options: Delete the oldest glossaries so the newest ones still fit in the Project
Split the glossaries across several Projects, one per language pair
Keep the files and name them clearly; retrieval expands capacity
Paste the most-used glossaries into the instructions and remove the files
explanation: C is correct: on paid plans, retrieval switches on as knowledge nears the limit, so Claude searches the files and capacity grows up to about ten times; clear names help it find them. A is wrong because it throws away references translators still use. B is wrong because a chat in one Project can't use another Project's files. D is wrong because instructions are for rules, and long reference text there buries them.

scenario: On a Team plan, a zoo education team shares its "School visits" Project with "Can edit" access. Colleagues who only need to chat in it keep changing its instructions by accident.
question: What is the best fix?
options: Unshare the Project and email everyone copies of its knowledge files
Add "Do not edit these instructions" to the top of the Project instructions
Move the instructions into each colleague's account instructions instead
Change their access to "Can view" so they can still use and see the Project
explanation: D is correct: "Can view" lets colleagues chat in the Project and see its knowledge and instructions without changing them. A is wrong because each person would then work from loose copies with no shared instructions. B is wrong because the note is just text, and edit access still lets anyone change it. C is wrong because account instructions apply to all their chats and drift apart as each person edits their own copy.

scenario: An executive assistant exports her boss's calendar to a file and uploads it to a Project every morning. Meetings often move during the day.
question: What is the better approach?
options: Connect Google Calendar to read the live schedule
Upload a fresh calendar export twice a day instead of once
Paste each day's calendar into the Project instructions
Keep one weekly export in knowledge and mention changes in chat
explanation: A is correct: a connector reads the live calendar through her account, so moved meetings show up as soon as they change. B is wrong because each upload is still a snapshot that goes stale between exports. C is wrong because instructions are for standing rules, and a daily paste is the same stale copy. D is wrong because chat mentions get missed, and the weekly file then contradicts them.

scenario: A florist group's events assistant on a Pro plan has Gmail connected with the default settings. She asks Claude to "send replies to all 12 wedding enquiries now".
question: What should she expect to happen?
options: Claude sends the 12 replies in one go because she asked for them
Claude can draft the replies in Gmail but cannot send any of them
Claude asks her to approve each send, so she reviews each draft
Claude sends the replies from the group's shared enquiries address
explanation: C is correct: with default settings, Claude asks for approval before sending, replying to or forwarding email, so she can check each draft before it goes. A is wrong because her request doesn't skip that default prompt. B is wrong because sending works once she approves it. D is wrong because the connector acts only through her own connected Google account, not a shared mailbox she hasn't connected.

scenario: A port authority planning officer has Google Drive connected. She needs a summary of a berth-allocation report in her manager's Drive that only the manager can open.
question: What is the best way to get the summary?
options: Ask Claude to request access to the report from her manager
Ask Claude to summarise the report from its title and folder name
Reconnect Drive using the authority's Drive administrator account
Ask her manager to share the report, or to run the summary herself
explanation: D is correct: Claude inherits her Drive permissions, so it can open only what her connected account can open; sharing the file fixes that. A is wrong because Claude doesn't send access requests on her behalf. B is wrong because a title gives Claude nothing real to summarise, so it would guess. C is wrong because using an administrator account to get round sharing defeats the permissions the manager set.

scenario: A consultant wants every Claude chat to use British spelling and lead with the recommendation, whatever the topic.
question: Where should this preference go?
options: The instructions of her largest client's Project
A style-guide file uploaded to each of her Projects
A reminder line at the start of each new chat
Her account instructions, in Settings > Your Claude
explanation: D is correct: account instructions apply to all her conversations, so a preference she wants everywhere belongs there. A is wrong because Project instructions apply only to chats in that Project. B is wrong because knowledge files are reference material, and she'd have to maintain a copy in each Project. C is wrong because retyping it in each chat is what standing instructions remove, and she will forget some days.

scenario: An IT consultancy bid team is writing the instructions for its client-proposals Project. Past drafts guessed at unclear tender requirements.
question: Which Project instruction is most effective?
options: Write polished, persuasive proposals in a confident, professional tone that impresses procurement teams
Write for procurement managers, lead with cost, follow the template, and list unclear points under 'Questions for the client'
Don't make assumptions or mistakes, and double-check each requirement carefully before you write
Follow the client's tender document closely and keep each proposal concise, clear and well organised
explanation: B is correct: it names the audience, the priority, the structure and what to do when information is missing, so Claude has specific actions to take. A is wrong because 'polished' and 'persuasive' leave Claude guessing what the team wants. C is wrong because banning mistakes gives no method, so the guessing carries on. D is wrong because 'concise and clear' names no audience, structure or fallback for unclear requirements.

scenario: A user's account instructions say "answer in bullet points", but her client-letters Project says to write full paragraphs. Her letters now come out in a mix of both.
question: What is the best fix?
options: Add 'ignore my account instructions' to each client letter she requests
Move the paragraph rule into her account instructions as well
Clear her account instructions whenever she works in the Project
Make the bullet rule conditional; keep letter format in the Project
explanation: D is correct: when two levels clash, make the broader rule conditional or remove it, so each rule applies where it fits. A is wrong because she must remember it in each request, and missed ones still come out as bullets. B is wrong because the paragraph rule would then fight the bullet rule in all her chats. C is wrong because clearing and restoring her preferences each time is fragile and easily forgotten.

scenario: A dental practice group updates its fee schedule. The reception team's Project now holds both last year's and this year's fee schedule.
question: What should the Project owner do?
options: Remove the old file and note the change in the Project instructions
Keep both files so the team can still look up last year's fees if asked
Rename the new file "FINAL" so Claude knows which one to use
Tell users to ignore the old file when they ask about fees
explanation: A is correct: one current version means one source, and a dated note tells users what changed. B is wrong because Claude may quote either schedule to a patient. C is wrong because a file name doesn't stop Claude reading and quoting the old figures. D is wrong because users can't control which file Claude draws on, so last year's fees still appear in answers.

scenario: A shared Project at a bookshop chain is used by 40 staff. Nobody has checked its files since it was created a year ago.
question: Which practice best keeps it reliable?
options: Give everyone "Can edit" so anyone can add files when they spot a gap
Delete the Project each year and rebuild it from the latest files
Name an owner, set a review date, and test set questions after updates
Ask each user to check the files they rely on and report problems
explanation: C is correct: an accountable owner, a regular review and a few test questions after each change keep a shared Project current. A is wrong because unmanaged edits add duplicates and conflicting versions. B is wrong because it discards working setup and still leaves nobody responsible. D is wrong because forty people checking their own files gives no single view, so the gaps between them go unnoticed.

scenario: The owner of a team Project at a garden centre has just replaced the leave policy file and updated the instructions.
question: What else should she do?
options: Leave it there; users will notice when the answers change
Ask users to re-upload the old policy in chats for comparison
Delete the old chats so nobody sees the old answers
Test common leave questions and tell users what changed
explanation: D is correct: testing standard questions confirms the Project now answers from the new policy, and telling users explains why answers changed. A is wrong because a silent change looks like an error, and nobody confirms it works. B is wrong because it brings the outdated policy back as a second source. C is wrong because past chats aren't the problem, and deleting them loses records people may need.

scenario: A coffee roaster's marketing lead pasted the company's 40-page brand guide into a Project's instructions, below the rules on voice, format and when to escalate.
question: How should she restructure the Project?
options: Leave the guide in the instructions, as instructions are read in each chat
Cut the guide down to its 10 key pages and keep it in the instructions
Move the guide into knowledge; keep the rules in the instructions
Remove the guide and upload it to each chat that needs brand detail
explanation: C is correct: instructions say how Claude behaves (voice, format, escalation), while reference documents belong in knowledge, which every chat in the Project can use. A is wrong because forty pages bury the few real rules. B is wrong because it still mixes reference text with rules and drops thirty pages of guidance. D is wrong because per-chat uploads repeat work and drift between versions.

scenario: An insurance broker names a Project after one marine client and writes the client's details in its description. In chats, Claude doesn't seem to know which client the work is for.
question: What should the broker change?
options: Rename the Project with the client's full legal name
Write the client details in the Project instructions
Expand the Project description with more client detail
Mention the client in the first chat so later chats pick it up
explanation: B is correct: Claude can't see a Project's name or description, so anything it needs must sit in the instructions or knowledge. A is wrong because a clearer name is still invisible to Claude. C is wrong because Claude doesn't read the description either, however detailed. D is wrong because chats in a Project don't share each other's conversations, so later chats won't know the client.

scenario: On a Team plan, a film festival's programme manager goes on leave for a month. One co-owner must keep the Project's files up to date while she is away; ten other staff only need to use it.
question: How should she set sharing before she leaves?
options: Give the co-owner "Can edit" and the ten staff "Can view"
Give everyone "Can edit" so anyone can fix an outdated file
Give everyone "Can view" and update the files when she is back
Give the co-owner "Can view" and have changes emailed to the manager
explanation: A is correct: the deciding constraint is that only one person needs to change the Project, so only the co-owner gets "Can edit" while the rest can still use and see it. B is the tempting option, but it lets ten more people change instructions and files. C is wrong because the files would sit stale for a month. D is wrong because the manager is away, so every change waits for her return.

scenario: A courier start-up updated its prohibited-items list this month. Its customer-help Project still holds last year's PDF, which Claude keeps quoting.
question: What should the Project owner do?
options: Upload the new PDF next to the old one so both are available
Remove the old PDF from knowledge, then upload the new one
Tell Claude in a chat that the list changed this month and why
Rename the old PDF "OLD - do not use" and upload the new one
explanation: B is correct: an upload is a fixed copy, so replacing it means removing the old file and adding the new one, leaving a single source. A is wrong because two versions are two sources, and Claude may quote either. C is wrong because a chat message stays in that chat and doesn't reach the Project's other chats. D is wrong because Claude can still read the renamed file and quote it.

scenario: A municipal events team works in one shared Project. Claude needs the latest version of a Google Doc listing road closures, which the team updates daily.
question: What is the best way to give Claude the current document?
options: Add the Doc from Drive to the shared Project's knowledge so it syncs
Use the Drive connector to open the Doc in each chat that needs it
Upload the Doc once a week and put the date in its file name
Copy the day's closures into the Project instructions each morning
explanation: B is correct: the deciding constraint is that the Project is shared, and Drive files can be added to knowledge only in private Projects, so the connector reads the live Doc in the chat. A is tempting, as an added Doc syncs, but not in a shared Project. C is wrong because a weekly upload is stale the next day. D is wrong because instructions hold rules, and a daily paste is easily missed.

scenario: A wine importer's sales assistant sets up a Project with three sources: a returns policy PDF that rarely changes, her Gmail inbox, and a price sheet in Google Drive updated weekly.
question: Which setup fits these sources best?
options: Upload the policy; connect Gmail and Drive for the inbox and price sheet
Upload the policy and the price sheet; connect Gmail for the inbox
Upload an inbox export and the price sheet; connect Drive for the policy
Upload the policy, the price sheet and a weekly export of the inbox
explanation: A is correct: upload what rarely changes and connect what keeps changing, so the policy sits in knowledge while the inbox and weekly sheet are read live. B is wrong because the uploaded price sheet goes stale within a week. C is wrong because it's reversed: the changing sources become stale snapshots while the stable policy is fetched live. D is wrong because a weekly inbox export is out of date by the next day.

scenario: A recycling company's site supervisor sometimes needs incident write-ups in the firm's set layout, from whichever chat she is working in. Code execution is on.
question: Where should the layout live?
options: In her account instructions, so each chat can use it
In the instructions of her site-operations Project
As a skill that loads when she asks for a write-up
In a saved note she pastes in each time it's needed
explanation: C is correct: a skill is a saved procedure that loads only when a task calls for it, in any chat, and skills need code execution, which is on. A is wrong because account instructions apply to all her chats, including those with nothing to do with incidents. B is wrong because Project instructions apply only inside that Project. D is wrong because pasting relies on her remembering, and copies drift.

scenario: An independent consultant wants British spelling everywhere, client A's terminology only in client A's work, and the firm's audit-report layout only when she asks for an audit report, for any client.
question: Which setup puts each rule at the right level?
options: Account: spelling. Client A Project: terms. Skill: audit layout
Account: spelling. Client A Project: terms and audit layout
Account: spelling and audit layout. Client A Project: terms
Account: spelling and client A terms. Skill: audit layout
explanation: A is correct: spelling applies everywhere, client A's terms to one client, and the layout to any client on request, which is what a skill does. B is the tempting option, but the deciding constraint is 'for any client': Project instructions would trap the layout in client A's work. C is wrong because account instructions would apply the layout to each chat. D is wrong because client A's terms would leak into other clients' work.

scenario: A housing developer's sales team no longer uses its "Show home launch" Project. An external consultant whose contract has ended still has "Can edit" access to it.
question: What should the Project owner do?
options: Archive the Project, which ends her access along with the team's
Remove her in the sharing settings, then archive it if wanted
Leave it as it is, since nobody is using the Project any more
Change her access to "Can view" and then archive the Project
explanation: B is correct: the deciding fact is that archiving keeps a Project's members and permission levels, so only removing her in sharing settings ends her access. A is the tempting option, but after archiving she would still reach its knowledge and chats. C is wrong because an unused Project is still open to every member. D is wrong because "Can view" still lets her read the instructions and knowledge after her contract has ended.

scenario: A water utility's customer team relies on a Project that answers billing-dispute questions and is reviewed each quarter. Mid-quarter, the regulator shortens the complaint-response deadline.
question: What should the Project owner do?
options: Wait for the quarterly review, which is when Project changes are made
Email users about the new deadline and update the Project at review
Replace the quarterly review with updates when users report errors
Update the files now, test, tell users, and keep the quarterly review
explanation: D is correct: the deciding constraint is that the source has changed, so the Project is wrong now; update it, test common questions and tell users, while the schedule catches slower drift. A is the tempting option, but Claude would quote the old deadline for weeks. B is wrong because users know the new deadline while Claude keeps answering with the old one. C is wrong because waiting for reports lets errors reach customers first.
